notes.text: The vote probability is the chance the base classifier returns the top class on one single noise draw, not the majority over many draws.
notes.quote: It is the probability that the base classifier returns the top class when you draw one single noise sample

notes.text: why Phi inverse and not a tail bound?
notes.answer: Neyman-Pearson makes the worst case a half space, and the distance from a Gaussian's centre to a half space of a given mass is exactly Phi inverse, so it is exact rather than a bound.

notes.text: Phi inverse rather than a Hoeffding tail bound because Neyman-Pearson makes the worst case a half space, and the distance from a Gaussian's centre to a half space of given mass is exactly Phi inverse.
notes.quote: the distance from the centre of a Gaussian to a half space of a given mass is exactly fee inverse of that mass

notes.text: A tail bound would be true but loose, and loose here means throwing away radius you had already earned.
notes.quote: It would just be loose, and loose here means you throw away radius that you actually earned

notes.text: Pushed far enough the trade-off ends in collapse: the base classifier can no longer see anything and the vote probability falls to chance.
notes.quote: at some point the base classifier can't see anything at all and the vote probability collapses to chance

notes.text: The paper sweeps sigma at 0.25, 0.5 and 1, and the 0.5 curve is the one everybody ends up plotting.
notes.quote: they sweep sigma at point two five, point five and one, and the point five curve is the one everybody ends up plotting

notes.text: The certificate is an ell two guarantee even though the slide states the threat model in the ell infinity norm, because Phi inverse of a Gaussian mass is a Euclidean distance.
notes.quote: the certificate we just derived is an ell two certificate. Fee inverse of a Gaussian mass is a Euclidean distance

notes.text: You can convert, since an ell two ball of radius r contains an ell infinity ball of radius r over root d, but that root d is brutal once d is a real image.
notes.quote: An ell two ball of radius r contains an ell infinity ball of radius r over root d

notes.text: When a paper quotes an ell infinity radius, check whether it converted or smoothed with a different distribution: uniform or Laplace noise gives an ell one or ell infinity certificate directly.
notes.quote: Different noise, different geometry, same Neyman Pearson skeleton underneath

notes.text: He said the deck is wrong here: the noise scale is sigma, the standard deviation, not the variance sigma squared, and he will fix the slide before posting it.
notes.quote: The noise scale is the standard deviation, not the variance. The deck is wrong there

notes.text: He tied the left column back to lecture two, where a published defense fell to a transfer attack in about fifteen minutes: empirical robustness is a claim about the attacks somebody happened to run.
notes.quote: Remember lecture two, when we broke that published defense in about fifteen minutes with a transfer attack?

notes.text: Exam hint: shown a table of robust accuracies and asked what is wrong with it, the answer he wants is that the attack was fixed and the defense tuned against it.
notes.quote: the attack was fixed and the defense was tuned against it

notes.text: does a certified radius survive fine tuning the base classifier?
If a certified number ever beats an empirical number on the same model the evaluation is broken; certified numbers come out smaller every single time.
notes.quote: If you ever see a certified number that beats an empirical number on the same model, something is broken in the evaluation

notes.text: He reframed the small certified number as a floor you can stand on, against the empirical number as a ceiling that may not exist at all.
notes.quote: A small honest number is a floor. The empirical number is a ceiling that may not even exist.

notes.text: Certified accuracy only means something at a stated radius, so find the radius column first when you read a table; papers do publish certified accuracies without one.
notes.quote: A certified accuracy without a radius attached is meaningless, and you will see it in papers anyway

notes.text: The guarantee degrades with dimension: at fixed accuracy the certified radius shrinks roughly like one over root d in ell infinity, tolerable on CIFAR and embarrassing on ImageNet.
notes.quote: The certified radius you can get at a fixed accuracy shrinks roughly like one over root d

notes.text: Certified robustness on high-resolution images is a research area rather than a tool, so his answer on certifying a production model is no, for sample cost first and dimension second.
notes.quote: It is a research area, it is not a tool you reach for.

notes.text: Where it does earn its keep is small inputs with high stakes: tabular medical data and control signals, where d is small and being wrong is expensive.
notes.quote: small inputs with high stakes. Tabular medical data, control signals, anything where d is small

notes.text: The guarantee is per input, not a property of the model: two images of the same class can have wildly different radii, which certified accuracy at one radius hides.
notes.quote: It is not a property of the model, it is a property of the model at that point
